Tash Kubra Zada was more a historian of philosophy than a philosopher. He wrote The Key to Happiness and Lamp of the Abode of Sovereignty, printed in Hyderabad: vol. 1 in 1328 AH and vol. 2 in 1329 AH. The work gives a critical account of the development of Muslim knowledge of the sciences. In it, he describes the “philosophical sciences” as “the true sciences that do not change with changing times, governments, or religions.” He places logic among the “divine sciences” and links philosophy with Sufism when he says that the philosophical sciences may be gained through rational investigation or through purification—meaning purification of the soul through spiritual discipline and struggle, that is, Sufism. In the terminology of early historians, classification into “classes” (tabaqat) was not based on social class in the modern sense. It usually meant chronological grouping. A “class” could therefore mean a generation of poets, hadith scholars, philosophers, and so on, with a generation usually spanning between ten and twenty years. Sometimes a geographical criterion was used, as Ibn Sa‘d did in his Great Book of Classes when he arranged biographies of the Companions according to the cities where they settled. See Ibn Sa‘d, Classes, Dar Sadir/Dar Beirut, 1957, Ihsan Abbas’s introduction, vol. 1, p. 12. Books of tabaqat, then, are specialized biographical works devoted to a particular group of historically important people. This form of writing among Arabs and Muslims goes back to the third century AH. Al-Waqidi may have been the first to write in this form, followed by his student Muhammad ibn Sa‘d; both wrote about hadith scholars. In the same century, many literary writers produced books on classes of poets, such as Ibn Sallam’s Classes, Ibn Qutayba’s Poetry and Poets, and Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s Classes of Poets. Later came works on the “classes” of physicians, sages, Shi‘is, Shafi‘is, and so on.↩︎

The history of Arabic literature gives us an example in which most of these personal, class, and ideological motives come together, along with a desire to flatter the ruling power. Abdallah ibn al-Mu‘tazz (247–296 AH), whose caliphate lasted no more than a day and part of another day, wrote a book called Classes of Poets, containing biographies of about 127 male and female poets from the Abbasid period. Three points about this book were noted by its editors, Abd al-Sattar Ahmad Farraj and Abbas Iqbal. First, Ibn al-Mu‘tazz ignores several of the greatest poets of his age, including Ibn al-Rumi (221–283 AH). He also ignores Ibn al-Rumi in his book al-Badi‘. Why, when Ibn al-Rumi was such an important poetic figure in the Arabic tradition? The editor and publisher Abd al-Sattar Farraj links this omission to two positions taken by Ibn al-Rumi. First, Ibn al-Rumi had satirized al-Mu‘tazz, the author’s father, after he was removed from the caliphate. Second, Ibn al-Rumi “was closely associated with al-Qasim ibn Ubayd Allah, one of Abdallah ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s enemies, who advised that he be arrested when al-Mu‘tadid died.” Here the motive is personal. Second, Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s book gives biographies of poets who praised or had connections with the Abbasid caliphs (...) and gathers poetry stamped with the outlook of poets dependent on Abbasid caliphs, ministers, and leading officials. It also tries to reveal the relationship between each poet and the person he praised (Abbas Iqbal). Here the motive is class-based and ideological. Third, the editors observe that despite Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s fame and the importance of his book, later biographers rarely mentioned it; “it was as though most of them did not know it.” Abd al-Sattar Farraj points to a convincing political reason: “al-Muqtadir returned to the caliphate and remained caliph for more than twenty years after Ibn al-Mu‘tazz was killed. There is no doubt that most transmitters do not favor someone from whom power has turned

There is no doubt that most transmitters do not favor someone from whom power has turned away and whom the events of time have brought down.” This is a case of flattering the ruling power. See Ibn al-Mu‘tazz, Classes of Poets, edited by Abd al-Sattar Ahmad Farraj, Dar al-Ma‘arif, Egypt, no date, pp. 10, 12, 583, 588.↩︎

The Arab world began using modern movable-type printing in the early eighteenth century. It is well known that the deacon Abdallah Zakhir of Aleppo established the first press using Arabic type in the town of al-Shuwayr in Lebanon in 1748. But Arabic movable type had already been used in Europe since the sixteenth century, beginning in 1514, when Pope Leo X opened the first Arabic press in Italy for printing religious books. Ibn Sina’s Canon may have been the first work from the Arabic intellectual heritage printed in Europe, in Rome in 1593. After that, Arabic heritage works continued to be published in European cities and capitals such as London, Paris, Leiden, Leipzig, Göttingen, Rome, Vienna, Berlin, and St. Petersburg—now Leningrad—before Arab countries themselves were able to make broad use of this form of printing. From the mid-nineteenth century onward, it spread through the Arab world for printing old and new books, magazines, and newspapers. See Jurji Zaydan, History of Arabic Literature, Cairo, 1911, vol. 4, pp. 54–56.↩︎

Some modern Salafis give a different account of the attempts by the “philosophers of Islam” to reconcile religion and philosophy. Their view contradicts the model presented here by Tawfiq al-Tawil, even though al-Tawil himself also follows a Salafi approach. Mahmud Qasim, for example, argues that Ibn Rushd merely brought religion together with Aristotle’s philosophy, without intending to defend philosophy itself. His aim, Qasim says, was to defend religion, as shown by the fact that he modified Aristotle’s philosophy and accepted from it only what he believed to be true. See Mahmud Qasim, Ibn Rushd, the Misrepresented Philosopher, Cairo, Anglo-Egyptian Bookshop, pp. 45–46. This disagreement among Salafis over how to understand the attempt to “reconcile” religion and philosophy in our philosophical heritage shows that the alleged reconciliation is not an objective historical reality, but a set of subjective interpretations imposed by shared ideological starting points. Most of these interpretations are also highly selective.↩︎

The method Taha Husayn followed in On Pre-Islamic Poetry was historical in a relative sense, but not historical in the full sense of the term. He tried to identify certain historical phenomena to support his view that pre-Islamic poetry was not actually pre-Islamic but later fabrication. We disagree with his conclusions, while still seeing his method as the beginning of a revolt against the traditionalist method.↩︎

Plato says in his famous dialogue (4A 2): “The ignorant do not concern themselves with philosophy and do not want to become wise, because the ugliness of ignorance lies in this: a person who is neither beautiful, complete, nor intelligent is nevertheless completely satisfied with himself and thinks he needs nothing, and therefore does not desire what he believes he does not need.” The “ignorant” in Plato’s formulation here are neither the gods nor the philosophers; they are the slaves. The judgment that a human being is not beautiful, complete, intelligent, and so on excludes philosophers and places a fixed metaphysical barrier before the development of the lower classes and before any possibility that they might reach the level of philosophy. Their ignorance is therefore treated as innate and unchangeable.↩︎
